<p>When you enter a toy store, the hundreds of colorful, noisy, and lit-up products on the shelves can be overwhelming. Often, parents think that the biggest, most functional, or most expensive toy is the best for their baby. However, the reality is quite different.</p><p>For babies, toys are not just a means of distraction; they are <strong>learning tools</strong> they use to understand the world, the laws of physics, and their own bodies. Choosing the right toy develops a child's imagination, motor skills, and intelligence. So, which toys should you choose according to your baby's months? Let's look at the most beneficial choices by period.</p><h2>0-3 months: Visual and auditory discoveries</h2><p>During this period, your baby explores the world more with their eyes and ears than with their hands. Since their vision is not fully formed, you should focus primarily on contrasting colors and gentle sounds.</p><ul><li><p><strong>Black-and-white contrast cards:</strong> Black-and-white geometric shapes attached to the side of the baby's crib or changing table develop visual focus and eye muscles.</p></li><li><p><strong>Soft rattles:</strong> Rattles that are not too loud and soft to the touch are ideal for the baby to search for the source of the sound (auditory development).</p></li><li><p><strong>Playmats:</strong> Looking at toys hanging from above during tummy time strengthens their neck and back muscles.</p></li></ul><h2>4-6 months: Grasping, exploring, and teething</h2><p>Now your baby purposefully reaches for objects, grasps them, and immediately puts them in their mouth to recognize them. The teething period also coincides with these months.</p><ul><li><p><strong>Safe teethers:</strong> BPA-free silicone or natural wooden teethers with different textures (bumpy, smooth) both soothe gum itching and teach different sensations.</p></li><li><p><strong>O-ball (Perforated balls):</strong> These lightweight balls with large holes are one of the perfect toys for a baby to easily grasp with small fingers.</p></li><li><p><strong>Crinkle cloth books:</strong> Soft and washable cloth books with rustling pages are a great tool for learning cause-and-effect relationships (I touch it and it makes a sound).</p></li></ul><h2>7-9 months: Cause-and-effect and active movement</h2><p>Babies who sit independently and slowly begin to crawl are now interested in how things work. They perform physical tests like "What happens if I throw this?" or "What sound will it make if I hit them together?"</p><ul><li><p><strong>Stacking cups:</strong> These simple cups are very functional for building towers, nesting inside each other, or simply banging together to make noise.</p></li><li><p><strong>Rolling toys and balls:</strong> To encourage crawling, you can use soft balls or cars that roll slightly away from them.</p></li><li><p><strong>Simple musical instruments:</strong> A small xylophone or a baby drum develops finger-eye coordination and forms a sense of rhythm.</p></li></ul><h2>10-12 months: Problem-solving and first steps</h2><p>Approaching one year of age, the baby now controls fine motor skills, tries to stand up, and begins to understand the purpose of objects.</p><ul><li><p><strong>Shape sorters:</strong> Passing shapes like circles, squares, and triangles through the appropriate holes requires great problem-solving (logic) skills and hand-eye coordination.</p></li><li><p><strong>Push walkers:</strong> Unlike classic walkers where you place the child inside, these toys that the baby pushes from behind provide great support for maintaining balance and taking first steps.</p></li><li><p><strong>Large building blocks (e.g., Lego Duplo):</strong> Repeatedly building and knocking down towers is both fun and the first foundation of creativity.</p></li></ul><h2>The golden rule for choosing toys: "Passive toy, active child"</h2><p>The main philosophy recommended by experts when buying toys is this: <strong>The more the toy does, the less the child does.</strong> Expensive toys that sing, spin, and flash colorful lights on their own when a button is pressed turn the baby into a mere passive observer. Instead, wooden blocks, cups, or simple cars engage the child's imagination – it is the child who makes the sounds, moves them, and builds the game.</p><h2>Record small successes with Anacan</h2><p>It is a great happiness to see the new skills your baby gains while playing with toys. You can track their individual development by adding motor leaps, such as building a tower for the first time, rolling a ball back to you, or putting a shape in the correct hole, to the "Development Tracker" section of the <strong>Anacan</strong> app. With the right toys and your love, your baby will make a new discovery every day!</p>
